# Solutions 04 (Topic 1) — Tutorial 01: Generative Modelling, EDA & SLR

*Questions: [`../04-tutorial-caschools-slr.md`](../04-tutorial-caschools-slr.md).*

---

**Q1.** "Generative modelling" means we assume the data were **generated by some underlying
(stochastic) mechanism**, and the regression is our **approximation of that data-generating process.**
The coefficients `b` are the **unknown true parameters** of that mechanism; we estimate them from a
sample, do inference to quantify our uncertainty about them, and use diagnostics to check whether the
assumed mechanism is plausible.

---

**Q2.** **False.** An SLR is **not exact** — it includes a random error term. The correct model is
`Y_i = b0 + b1*X_i + e_i`. Without `e_i` every point would lie perfectly on the line, which never
happens with real (stochastic) data; the line gives only the **conditional average** `E[Y|X]`.

---

**Q3.** `e_i` absorbs (1) the effect of **other explanatory variables not in the model** and (2)
**pure random noise.** We can't observe it because it's defined relative to the **true** population
line (`b0`, `b1`), which is unknown — the best we can compute is the **residual** (from the estimated
line), which is only a stand-in for `e_i`.

---

**Q4.** Any two of: (1) `ggpairs()` **picks the appropriate plot per variable type** (scatter,
box/violin, bar) automatically; (2) it shows each variable's **distribution on the diagonal** (base
`pairs()` just labels it); (3) instead of duplicating the mirrored scatterplots, it reports the
**correlation coefficient** (or another informative summary) in the upper triangle. Net: more
information, less redundancy.

---

**Q5.** **Correct:** "Each additional **\$1000** of district average income is **associated with** an
increase of about **1.94** points in the average reading score, on average across districts." The
"**raises**" version is wrong because it asserts **causation** from **observational** data — we can
only claim association.

---

**Q6.** (a) **Yes, significant.** The 95% CI `(1.75, 2.13)` **excludes 0**, and `p < 0.05` — both say
reject `H0: b_income = 0`. (b) The `lm` p-values come from **classical theoretical** approximations
(the t/normal sampling distribution), **not** bootstrapping.

---

**Q7.** The distribution of **`b1_hat`, the estimator of the slope.** It is not the distribution of
`Y` (that's the response scatter), nor of the true `b1` (a fixed unknown constant, not random), nor of
`X` (the predictor, treated as fixed). The sampling distribution describes how the **estimate** would
vary from sample to sample.

---

**Q8.** **Resample the observed districts with replacement**, each resample the **same size `n`** as
the data; refit `lm(read ~ income)` each time and store the slope — repeat **B = 10000** times to build
`boot_slope`. The spread of those 10000 slopes approximates the sampling distribution; a **90% CI** is
the **5th and 95th percentiles** of `boot_slope` (leaving 5% in each tail).
